nodes.question: In what context is the model employed in the study?
nodes.answer: The model is employed in the context of non-cooperative dynamic games.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract The purpose of the paper is to study how research and development (R&D) into adaptation technologies and mitigation activity for the reduction of emissions can influence participation in International Environmental Agreements (IEAs). Both mitigation and adaptation are supposed to be a public good because both produce the benefit of all countries. The model is employed in the context of non-coopera- tive dynamic games. Countries are involved in a two-stage game. In the first stage, each country decides upon its participation in the agreement, that means collec- tively deciding their mitigation and adaptation policies. In the second stage, coun- tries decide on their mitigation strategies and investment in R&D, either individu- ally or collectively, depending on their decision in the first stage. Members of the agreement fully share their knowledge about adaptation capacity and there is the assumption that some knowledge unintentionally spills over between a signatory and a non-signatory country and between two non-signatory countries. nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: What do the forms of conflict management and cooperation define in the context of local interactive governance?
nodes.answer: They define the nature of local interactive governance and its capacities for promoting sustainable development and democracy.
nodes.paragraph: Whilethe impact of these forms of con ict management, bridge- building, or even cooperation may vary, they altogether de ne the nature of local interactive governance and itscapacities for promoting sustainable development and democracy. Keywords Interactive governance /C1Local climate governance /C1Civil society /C1 Local administration /C1 Collaboration Introduction While environmental challenges are high on the publicagenda, they have raised many questions concerning the ability of society and politics to cope with them. Much ofthe attention goes either to government action or to the various forms of people S reaction, namely protest on the streets and at the voting ballots. Especially liberaldemocracies, claiming to bridge people S will and institu- tional politics, get distressed by the massive challenges of the environmental crisis. The respective routines andinstitutions of democratic governance, as well as their methods of intermediating between institutional politics and the people, are being subjected to scrutiny. There is asearch for more interactive forms and proceedings that can mitigate con ict and dissent and facilitate the creation of legitimate and ef cient environmental politics. This calls for a relational approach (Evers & von Essen, 2019 & 2024 ), that takes up the roles of civic engagement and civil society actors as part of a wider complex interplay between state (political and administrative institutions), civil soci- ety, and economy.

nodes.answer: The central question addressed in the final chapter is: To what degree does a more interactive governance also mean a more democratic governance?

nodes.id: Subtopic:Governance|Peace, justice and strong institutions|Good governance|Decentralized governance models_qna_004
nodes.label: Governance and participation
nodes.question: What is the central concept discussed in modern governance according to Kooiman?
nodes.answer: The central concept is the altered relationships between state governance and the addressees in society, often referred to as new governance.
nodes.paragraph: The observation and analysis of alterations in gover- nance by increasing ways and new forms of participation especially but not only in liberal democratic systems and their political administrations, takes place in the theoretical literature under varying headings. The mention of newgovernance as modern governance (Kooiman, 1993 ) referred quite generally to altered relationships between state governance and the addressees in society. A centralconcept was that of cross-sectoral policy networks (Marin & Mayntz, 1991 ). In the subsequent international discus- sion, four terms have become established: collaborative governance (Ansell & Gash, 2007 ; Hofstadt et al., 2022 ), intersectoral governance (McQueen et al., 2013 ; Gonser & Schmid, 2023 ), interactive governance (Tor ng et al., 2019 ), and intermediation (Evers & von Essen, 2024 Despite all the differences in detail, there remains a greataf nity between these concepts. The common fundamental idea can be formulated as follows: They understand gov- ernance as a question of development and dealing withdifferent forms of mutual in uence and coordination between participants from the state sector, civil society, and the economy their involvement in the preparation ofconcepts, in decision-making, and in the process of their implementation.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Governance|Peace, justice and strong institutions|Good governance|Decentralized governance models_qna_005
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: What relationship exists between multi-level governance and local innovations?
nodes.answer: Multi-level governance serves as a framework for interactions between local innovations and central impulses, facilitating both hierarchical and collaborative interactions.
nodes.paragraph: What is now demanded in the concepts for intersectoral/ interactive/collaborative governance is the upgrading ofelements that are mostly given lesser importance in the classical forms of liberal representative democracy. These elements can be brie y summarised in four points: The stronger involvement of participants and interests that are particularly affected in the respective area of apolitical intervention. The term stakeholder is very often utilised for this. Opportunities for citizens to participate in various sectors of services (health, education, and culture) as kind of co-producers (Brandsen et al., 2018 ) in their design and functioning individually and through their own organisations. Ideally, this can take place even before the implementation phase by citizens as co-initiators (Stougaard, 2021 ). The joint search for situation-speci C variants and concepts, which could thereby deviate from samenessin the sense of centrally decreed uniformity without, however, calling into question equal basic rights. There is a close relationship here with the concept of multi-level governance , which not only functions hierarchi- cally, but also as a reference framework for interactions between local innovations and central impulses (e.g.through social innovations and model programmes) (Evers & Ewert, 2021 ).
